title: Assign the same tags that later invalidation targets
businessContext: Review a focused Next.js application change before it reaches production. The proposed file below contains the defect or unsupported assumption; external application services, where imported, are integration boundaries.
problemStatement: Review the proposed lib/products.ts change. Identify the incorrect framework assumption, propose a minimal corrected implementation, and provide evidence for the selected version scope and its 15/16 differences. Explain the interview variation after solving the base task. This is a framework code review: actual rendering, routing and cache behavior must be checked in a real Next.js build, not a browser function sandbox.
constraints: Preserve the stated user behavior and keep trust boundaries explicit.
Use the selected version’s documented API; do not suppress build/type failures to hide the defect.
Cache two entities and a list in a production server.
Invalidate an entity tag and observe the affected representation.
Invalidate the list tag after membership changes and verify unrelated domains remain warm.
candidateTasks: Add actionable line-level review comments explaining impact and correction.
Write the corrected file in the local IDE copy; split annotated companion files where instructed.
Record actual build/request/navigation evidence against the acceptance checks and compare version notes.
hints: Invalidating a name that was never assigned does not refresh the intended entry.
Cache two entities and a list in a production server.
alternativeApproaches: Include trusted tenant scope in tag names and use bounded server-owned identifiers. Prevent a user-controlled webhook from invalidating every tenant, and monitor invalidation fan-out.
commonMistakes: Verifying only next dev when the behavior depends on production rendering or bundling.
Treating a visible UI state, matcher or TypeScript type as a substitute for server-side validation and authorization.
